content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all four blind responses the settled symbolic reading is that the bill of divorcement represents God's judicial severance of His covenant with unfaithful Israel: spiritual adultery (idolatry) triggers a covenant lawsuit whose historical expression is exile, with prophetic hope of restoration/remarriage. Response A also lists a minority legal-typological view (God's divorce of Israel created a Deuteronomy 24 no-return problem resolved by Christ's death) and all note the dominant non-symbolic legal-ethical use in Deuteronomy and the Gospels.","book_summary":"The book identifies the bill of divorcement as the covenant lawsuit executed — the wife sent out of the house, i.e., exile and scattering. It adds a dual moral valence: divorce is hated when it betrays the covenant wife (Malachi 2) but commanded when the union is itself fornication, a marriage God never joined (Ezra 10). It further asserts that God gave Israel the bill and 'answered His own no-return rule' (Deut 24:4) at the cross.","consensus_core_identification":"Divorce/bill of divorcement symbolizes God's judicial covenant severance from unfaithful Israel for spiritual adultery, expressed historically in exile, with restoration anticipated.","book_core_identification":"The bill of divorcement is the executed covenant lawsuit — exile and scattering of the unfaithful wife — with divorce hated when treacherous but commanded against unlawful unions, and the Deut 24 no-return barrier resolved at the cross.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUPERSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book broadens the symbol beyond the consensus in two ways: (1) it incorporates commanded divorce of illegitimate unions (Ezra 10's putting away of foreign wives) into the symbolic field, giving divorce a positive, mandated valence that no consensus response includes among its symbolic meanings; (2) it commits to the legal-typological claim that Christ's death at the cross resolves the Deuteronomy 24:4 no-return prohibition, allowing divorced Israel's remarriage — a position Response A explicitly flags as a minority (Two-House/messianic) reading, not the mainstream one. The consensus core (covenant lawsuit, exile for spiritual adultery) is fully retained.","material_contradiction":"None. The book affirms rather than denies the consensus identification; its additions elevate a recognized minority reading and add the Ezra 10 commanded-divorce case, but nothing in the entry requires rejecting the consensus core.","rationale":"Both the consensus and the book identify the same central referent: God's judicial divorce of unfaithful Israel resulting in exile/scattering (Jer 3:8; Isa 50:1). The book therefore does not diverge at the core. However, it materially changes the boundary and precision of the symbol. It adds cases the consensus does not treat symbolically (commanded dissolution of fornication-unions per Ezra 10, contrasted with hated treacherous divorce per Mal 2), and it asserts as settled the cross-resolution of the Deut 24:4 no-return rule, which the blind responses treat as a minority position. This is real refinement — an extension of covered cases and adoption of a stronger legal-typological mechanism — not mere wording difference, and not a replaced referent.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the core is identical, the cross-resolution claim is already catalogued as a listed minority alternative in Response A, and the Malachi 2/Ezra 10 material could be read as immaterial ethical detail rather than a change to the symbol's extension. If the dual-valence and cross claims are treated as elaboration rather than boundary change, the differences reduce to detail.","confidence":"medium"}
